JAMA Neurology . https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the CC-BY License. jamaneurol-e212120.pdf Key Points Question Are different patterns of intracranial injury on head computed tomography associated with prognosis after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)? Findings In this cohort study, subarachnoid hemorrhage, subdural hematoma, and contusion often co-occurred and were associated with both incomplete recovery and more severe impairment out to 12 months after injury, while intraventricular and/or petechial hemorrhage co-occurred and were associated with more severe impairment up to 12 months after injury; epidural hematoma was associated with incomplete recovery at some points but not with more severe impairment. Some intracranial hemorrhage patterns were more strongly associated with outcomes than previously validated demographic and clinical variables. Meaning In this study, different pathological features on head computed tomography carried different implications for mild traumatic brain injury prognosis to 1 year. molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI) and recovery outcomes
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The study identifies specific pathological features and patterns of intracranial hemorrhage on head computed tomography (CT), along with demographic and clinical factors, that are associated with varying post-TBI recovery outcomes, as measured by GOSE scores. While not detailing a molecular mechanism, it infers that these structural injuries and pre-existing conditions contribute to varying degrees of recovery. Specific injury mechanisms are suggested: subarachnoid hemorrhage, contusion, and subdural hemorrhage may arise from linear acceleration or deceleration, whereas intraventricular and petechial hemorrhage likely result from rotational acceleration or deceleration, with IVH indicating more severe rotational forces.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Different pathological features and subtypes of intracranial hemorrhage on head computed tomography (CT) in mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) carry distinct prognostic implications over 1 year. Granular CT findings proved superior to binary CT results, demonstrating varying odds ratios for prognosis. For instance, the Contusion, Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH), and/or Subdural Hematoma (SDH) cluster consistently linked to both incomplete recovery (GOSE <8) and unfavorable outcomes (GOSE <5) across all time points. Intraventricular and/or petechial hemorrhage significantly associated with greater degrees of unfavorable outcomes. In contrast, Epidural Hematoma was associated only with incomplete recovery at earlier time points (2 weeks and 3 months) and not with more severe unfavorable outcomes. Age and education levels also showed varying associations, with older age and lower education correlating with worse outcomes, particularly for more severe outcomes (GOSE <5). The Rotterdam CT score, typically used for moderate to severe TBI, demonstrated limited utility in mTBI due to minimal variability. The study's enriched complicated mTBI cohort (37% positive CT rate) enabled this granular analysis.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study specifically investigated mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI, GCS scores 13-15), addressing a knowledge gap regarding the prognostic importance of CT abnormalities in this population. It identified distinct CT phenotypes (e.g., Contusion, SAH, and/or SDH cluster; Intraventricular and/or Petechial Hemorrhage; Epidural Hematoma) through Hierarchical Cluster Analysis and Multiple Correspondence Analysis. These phenotypes showed specific associations with different aspects of recovery (incomplete recovery vs. greater unfavorable outcomes) and across various post-injury time points, demonstrating superior prognostic specificity compared to previously validated demographic and clinical variables. For example, Epidural Hematoma specifically linked to incomplete recovery but not more severe unfavorable outcomes, while Intraventricular and/or Petechial Hemorrhage were strongly tied to greater degrees of unfavorable outcomes. These findings were reproducible across two independent cohorts, underscoring their consistent specificity for prognostic stratification in mTBI.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients 17 years and older with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI, Glasgow Coma Scale scores 13-15), who presented to emergency departments at US and European trauma centers and underwent head CT imaging within 24 hours of TBI. This includes cohorts from the TRACK-TBI study (1935 patients) and the CENTER-TBI study (2594 patients), focusing particularly on those with complicated mTBI (intracranial hemorrhage on head CT).
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The identification of specific pathological CT features and demographic factors in mTBI serves as crucial prognostic indicators for recovery up to 12 months post-injury. These routinely obtained imaging findings and clinical data can help predict adverse outcomes, including incomplete recovery and more severe impairment, enabling the identification of patients at higher risk. This information is vital for personalized care, improving clinical trial design, facilitating triage to TBI-specific education, and ensuring systematic follow-up for mTBI patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The identified CT features and demographic factors offer significant diagnostic utility and prognostic stratification. They classify patients into risk categories for adverse outcomes following mTBI, indicating higher risk for incomplete recovery and unfavorable outcomes (e.g., with contusion, SAH, SDH, IVH, petechial hemorrhage). Epidural hematoma, while associated with incomplete recovery, indicates a comparatively lower risk for greater degrees of unfavorable outcomes.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of the identified CT features and prognostic indicators is strongly supported by their external validation and striking replication across two large, independent longitudinal observational cohorts: TRACK-TBI (US) and CENTER-TBI (Europe). The CT imaging phenotypes, derived from Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) and Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), were nearly identical and highly reproducible across both cohorts. Associations found using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) models also showed consistent findings, reinforcing the reliability. While the study benefited from advances in CT technology, the Rotterdam CT score 1 exhibited minimal variability in the mTBI population, indicating it is not a reliable measure for differentiating severity within mild TBI.
